newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Iraqi oil buys French, Australian wheat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraqi oil buys French, Australian wheat.

text.p: Iraq bought 300,000 tonnes of wheat from France and Australia on Thursday in deals worth nearly $40 million and thought to be the country's biggest food purchase in six years, European grain traders said.
Iraq bought the wheat with money raised from oil exports under a pact with the United Nations to provide relief from sanctions imposed after it invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Grain traders said the purchase followed several days of negotiations and Iraq was already talking about buying another 100,000 tonnes of wheat, this time from any producing country.
"They've bought, now we will see how much more can be done," an international grains trader said.
Wheat is due to start reaching the Iraqi Gulf port of Umm Qasr in January.

Iraq has said wheat will make up more than half of the two million tonnes of commodities it will buy with cash raised from oil exports which resumed on Monday. Other goods include rice, sugar, vegetable oils, detergent and soap.
Iraq is allowed to export enough oil to raise $2 billion in renewable six-month steps, while the remainder of the sanctions continue to apply.
About half the money raised will be deducted for U.N. costs, reparations and a special programme for Kurds in the north of Iraq.
Word of an important grain deal spread through markets early on Thursday when news of the first 100,000 tonnes of French wheat helped to drive grain futures prices higher in London.
LIFFE wheat futures closed around a pound sterling higher at 96.50 pounds ($160) a tonne.
Traders said Iraq bought the French wheat for $195 to $200 a tonne, including about $45 a tonne for freight and costs associated with the strictly monitored oil-for-food deal.
It bought lower-quality Australian wheat for $171-173 a tonne.
France, which has lent conditional support to Iraq's calls for a complete halt to U.N. sanctions, is expected to reap a number of oil and grain deals in return.
French oil companies Elf Aquitaine and Total have already signed agreements to buy Iraqi crude under the U.N. scheme.
Australia was Iraq's biggest wheat supplier before the Gulf crisis erupted in 1990 and hopes to sell 100,000 tonnes a month.
But the United States, Iraq's second wheat supplier before 1990 and its main Gulf War enemy, is unlikely to find favour.
Traders said Iraq was also rumoured to be buying wheat from Argentina this week but no deals were confirmed.
The Argentine government said last week it thought exporters had placed 80,000 tonnes of wheat with Iraq, but traders said deals were hard because rain was making Argentine wheat expensive.
